subject: Engelska
title: Writing: sentence structure and common mistakes
sourceSummary: English word order in statements and questions, the most common Swedish-English mistakes, and how to link sentences together with and, but and because.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has the correct word order?
questions.opener: English sticks firmly to the order subject - verb - object, even when the sentence starts with a time expression.
questions.explanation: In English, the subject comes before the verb: "I play football". Unlike some other languages, you do not swap the order of subject and verb just because the sentence starts with a time expression — that is why "On Mondays play I football" is wrong.

questions.opener: Questions in present simple need an auxiliary verb — and it comes first.
questions.explanation: The question word comes first, then the auxiliary verb do/does, then the subject and the verb: "Where do you live?". "Where live you?" follows the wrong word order and does not work in English.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly states someone's age in English?
questions.opener: Some languages use a different verb than English does when talking about age.
questions.explanation: In English, the verb "be" is used for age: "I am 13 years old". "I have 13 years" is a literal translation from another language and sounds wrong in English.

questions.opener: Check who is doing the action — which negative form goes with "he"?
questions.explanation: With he/she/it, "doesn't" is used, and after doesn't the verb stands in its base form: "He doesn't like homework". "He don't" is one of the most common mistakes, and "doesn't likes" conjugates the verb twice.

questions.prompt: Choose the best linking word: "I stayed at home ___ I was ill."
questions.opener: The second part explains why the first part happened.
questions.explanation: "Because" gives a reason, and being ill is the reason for staying home. "But" would show a contrast, which does not fit here.

questions.prompt: Which sentence joins the two ideas best: "I like football." + "I don't like tennis."
questions.opener: The two sentences say different things — which linking word shows a contrast?
choices: I like football and I don't like tennis.
I like football but I don't like tennis.
I like football because I don't like tennis.
I like football, I don't like tennis.
questions.explanation: "But" is used when two parts contrast with each other, like liking against not liking. "Because" would mean that one is the reason for the other, which is not the case here.

questions.prompt: Correct the four errors: "Hi! My name is Lisa and I have 13 years. My brother he don't like school. On Saturdays go I to my friend. Where you live?"
questions.opener: Look for age, the negative form, word order in a statement, and word order in a question.
questions.answer: Hi! My name is Lisa and I am 13 years old. My brother doesn't like school. On Saturdays I go to my friend. Where do you live?
steps: "I have 13 years" → "I am 13 years old". English uses the verb "be" for age and adds "old".
"My brother he don't like" → "My brother doesn't like". The subject should only appear once, and he/she/it takes doesn't + the verb in its base form.
"On Saturdays go I" → "On Saturdays I go". The subject comes before the verb in English even after a time expression.
"Where you live?" → "Where do you live?". Questions in present simple need the auxiliary verb do/does after the question word.

questions.prompt: What rules and common mistakes should you check when you write in English?
questions.opener: A checklist to go through before you hand in your text.
questions.answer: Word order: subject - verb - object (I play football) · the subject comes before the verb even after a time expression (Every day I read, not Every day read I). Questions: question word + do/does + subject + verb in base form (Where do you live? Does she play?) · with "be" you swap the order instead (Are you tired?). Common mistakes: I am 13 years old (not I have 13 years) · he/she/it doesn't (not he don't) · after doesn't/didn't the verb stands in its base form · don't forget -s in he plays, she watches · don't repeat the subject (My brother he...). Linking words: and = adds information · but = shows a contrast · because = gives a reason · so = shows a result. Always read through your text one last time and check the verbs.
